chapters.title: Work and Energy
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the concepts of kinetic energy, work done by forces, and the work-energy theorem. It explores how forces change the kinetic energy of particles and systems, and lays the groundwork for understanding potential energy and energy conservation.

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_1>>
If a car hits you at 10 km/h versus 100 km/h, it's not just 10 times worse — it's actually 100 times worse. Why? The answer is hiding in something called kinetic energy — the energy an object carries simply because it is moving. <<FOCUS:ball-slow>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_1:speed_squared_comparison>> Here are two identical balls. This one moves at speed v, and this one moves at double that speed — 2v. <<TRACE:ball-slow>> <<FOCUS:ball-fast>> Now here's the critical question: if speed doubles, does the kinetic energy double too? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:energy-bar-slow>> Watch these energy bars. The slow ball has 1 unit of kinetic energy. The fast ball — moving at twice the speed — has not 2 units, but 4. <<POINT:energy-bar-slow>> <<PAUSE:short>> The energy of a moving object is half its mass multiplied by its speed multiplied by itself — speed squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:energy-bar-fast>> Four times the energy for double the speed. That's the squared relationship — and it's why that faster car is so much more dangerous. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> The energy of a moving object is half its mass times its speed times itself — that is, speed squared. We write it as KE equals one-half m v squared. <<PAUSE:short>> Mass matters too — a heavier ball at the same speed carries more energy. But mass scales the energy once; speed squares it. <<POINT:ball-slow>> <<FOCUS:energy-bar-fast>> So here's the big takeaway to lock in: double the speed — four times the energy. Triple the speed — nine times the energy. Speed squared, every time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now you know why that faster car is not 10 times worse — it's 100 times worse. The square is not a detail; it's the whole story.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_2>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's something strange: you can hold a heavy bag of groceries for an hour, arms aching, muscles burning — and according to physics, you've done exactly zero work. How is that possible? <<FOCUS:block>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_2:work_angle_diagram>> The key is motion. Physics defines work only when a force actually moves something. No movement, no work — no matter how hard you strain. <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> Now watch this. Imagine you push this block with a force F at an angle — not straight along the ground, but tilted upward. <<TRACE:force-arrow>> The block only slides along the ground — horizontally. So here's the real question: does all of your push count as work? <<TRACE:displacement-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-component-horizontal>> Only the part of your force that actually points in the direction of motion does the pushing. That's this horizontal component — F cosθ. The upward part? It just presses into the ground and does nothing useful. <<TRACE:force-component-horizontal>> <<POINT:force-component-horizontal>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle-label>> That angle θ is between your force and the direction of travel — marked right here. Work is force times distance, but only the component along the motion counts. <<PAUSE:short>> Work is the size of the force, multiplied by the distance moved, multiplied by the cosine of the angle between them — because only the part of the force along the motion counts. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W = F \cos\theta \cdot d|id=eq-1|boxed>> So: work equals F cosθ times d. If you push perfectly along the motion, θ is zero, cosθ is one, and every bit of your force counts. If you push perfectly sideways to the motion, θ is ninety degrees, cosθ is zero — zero work. Just like holding that grocery bag. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:ke-initial-bar>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_2:work_energy_bar_diagram>> Now here comes the beautiful part. What actually happens to the object when work gets done on it? <<PAUSE:long>> Look at this: the object starts with some kinetic energy — KE₁. Then the net force does work on it. That work flows directly into the object's kinetic energy. <<TRACE:work-bar>> <<TRACE:work-bar>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:equals-annotation>> And the final kinetic energy KE₂ is exactly KE₁ plus all that work. The work done by ALL forces combined equals the change in kinetic energy. That is the work-energy theorem. <<POINT:equals-annotation>> <<PAUSE:short>> The total work done by all forces together equals exactly how much the kinetic energy changes — that's the work-energy theorem in one line. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = KE_2 - KE_1|id=eq-2|boxed>> Notice: it's the NET work — the total from every single force acting. One individual force doesn't change the kinetic energy on its own; they all have to be added up first. <<POINT:ke-final-bar>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So going back to our grocery bag: the bag doesn't move, so the force does zero work, so its kinetic energy never changes — it stays at rest. The theorem holds perfectly. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_3>>
Imagine you're holding a heavy suitcase, arms aching, muscles burning — and according to physics, you've done exactly zero work. How is that possible? <<FOCUS:displacement-vector>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_3:work_angle_diagram>> The key is direction. Physics only credits you with work when your force actually shoves the object along the direction it moves. Holding a suitcase still? Your force is upward; the suitcase isn't moving at all — zero displacement, zero work. Now imagine pushing a box across the floor, but your push is angled — like leaning into a trolley handle. Your force points diagonally, but the box only moves horizontally. <<TRACE:force-vector>> <<FOCUS:force-component>> The angle between your force and the displacement is θ. Only this horizontal slice of your force — F cosθ — actually does the pushing. That's the only part that counts. <<PAUSE:short>> So work equals force times displacement times cosine of the angle between them. Only the component of force along the motion counts. <<POINT:angle-arc>> <<PAUSE:short>> Work equals force times displacement times cosine of the angle between them — only the component of force along the motion counts. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W = Fr\cos\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:zero-work-label>> Here's the satisfying extreme: what if the force is perfectly perpendicular to motion — like gravity on a satellite orbiting Earth? The angle is 90°, cosine of 90° is zero, and boom — zero work done, no matter how large the force. <<POINT:zero-work-label>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_3:gravity_path_diagram>> Now here's a deeper question: a ball rolls from point A down to point B — sometimes along a steep straight slope, sometimes along a long winding curve. Does gravity do more work on the winding path because the ball travels further? <<TRACE:curved-path>> <<TRACE:curved-path>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:height-h>> The answer is no — both paths give exactly the same work. Watch why: gravity pulls straight down, and only the vertical drop h matters. The sideways wandering of the path cancels itself out completely. <<POINT:height-h>> <<FOCUS:gravity-arrow>> Gravity's work is simply weight times height dropped: mg times h. That's it. A zigzag path and a straight drop land on the same answer as long as A and B are the same two points. <<PAUSE:short>> Gravity's work is simply the weight of the object multiplied by the vertical height it descends — the path shape doesn't matter at all. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W_{\text{gravity}} = mgh|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:straight-path>> This is a powerful idea: when a force is constant, the work it does between two points depends only on those endpoints — not on the winding road taken between them. <<TRACE:straight-path>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So remember two things: work is F r cosθ — only the along-the-motion part of your force counts. And for a constant force like gravity, the path is irrelevant — only where you start and where you finish.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_4>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_4:two_charged_particles>> Two charged particles sitting in space — nobody touches them, no external force at all — and yet they suddenly start speeding up, gaining kinetic energy out of nowhere. Where on Earth did that energy come from? <<FOCUS:particle-A>> Here's our setup: particle A on the left, particle B on the right, one negative, one positive. They attract each other. <<POINT:particle-A>> B pulls A to the right with force F-AB, and A pulls B to the left with force F-BA. These are Newton's third-law partners — equal in size, exactly opposite in direction. <<TRACE:force-on-A>> <<TRACE:force-on-A>> Now here's the trap most people fall into: equal and opposite forces... their work must cancel out, right? The total work should be zero? <<POINT:force-on-B>> <<POINT:force-on-B>> <<PAUSE:long>> Watch what actually happens. A moves toward B — displacement to the right. B moves toward A — displacement to the left. Both particles are actually moving! <<TRACE:displacement-A>> <<TRACE:displacement-A>> Force on A points right. A moves right. That's work done IN THE SAME direction — W-AB is positive. Force on B points left. B moves left. Also the same direction — W-BA is also positive! <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:work-label-B>> So both forces do positive work. The total work by internal forces is not zero — it's the sum of two positive numbers. That's where the kinetic energy came from. <<PAUSE:short>> The forces cancel as vectors — F-AB plus F-BA equals zero — but work is force times displacement, and the displacements are also in opposite directions, so the negatives multiply and both contributions are positive. The works do NOT cancel. <<POINT:force-on-A>> <<POINT:force-on-A>> <<PAUSE:short>> The total work on the system is the sum of work by every force — internal ones included — and that total equals the change in the whole system's kinetic energy. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W_{\text{total}} = W_{AB} + W_{BA} = \Delta KE_{\text{system}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> This is the work-energy theorem for a system: the total work done by ALL forces — internal and external — equals the change in the system's total kinetic energy. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:particle-A>> So the big takeaway: internal forces between particles can absolutely increase a system's kinetic energy — even when there is no external force at all. The energy was stored in the configuration of the particles, and the internal forces released it as motion. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_5>>
<<FOCUS:velocity-arrow-a>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_5:two_particle_system>> Two charged particles fly away from each other — and something strange happens. They slow down, stop, then come rushing back. When they return to exactly where they started, they're moving at exactly the same speed as before. So where did the energy go while they were slowing down? <<TRACE:velocity-arrow-a>> <<FOCUS:config-1-label>> Here are our two particles, A and B, at what we'll call Configuration 1. Both are moving apart — these arrows show their velocities. The system has kinetic energy K₁. <<POINT:config-1-label>> <<FOCUS:config-2-label>> But they attract each other — that pull acts like a brake. As they move to Configuration 2, both arrows shrink. Less speed. Less kinetic energy — now only K₂, which is less than K₁. <<TRACE:config-2-label>> <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> Watch the energy bars. KE has dropped. But here's the key question: has that energy simply vanished from the universe? <<POINT:ke-bar>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:config-1-label>> No — it hasn't vanished at all. The particles eventually return to Configuration 1, moving at exactly the original speeds. K₁ is back, fully restored. Energy that seemed lost was just... waiting. <<TRACE:config-1-label>> <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> So we need a new kind of energy — one that rises when kinetic energy falls, and falls when kinetic energy rises. Energy that depends not on speed, but on the arrangement — the configuration — of the particles. <<POINT:pe-bar>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:attraction-arrow>> We call it potential energy. And notice: it's not the energy of particle A, nor of particle B alone. It belongs to the pair — to the gap between them, to their configuration. Change the arrangement, change the potential energy. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> Watch the trade-off: as the particles separate toward Configuration 2, KE shrinks and PE grows — by exactly the same amount. As they return, PE shrinks and KE recovers. The total stays constant. <<TRACE:ke-bar>> <<POINT:ke-bar>> The drop in kinetic energy exactly equals the rise in potential energy — so if you add them together, you always get the same number. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Delta KE = -\Delta PE \quad \Longrightarrow \quad KE + PE = \text{constant}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> This is the equation that captures it: the drop in kinetic energy equals the rise in potential energy. Or equivalently, KE plus PE is constant — that's conservation of energy, already hiding in this simple picture. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So the key idea to lock in: when kinetic energy decreases because of the force between two particles, that energy isn't lost — it's stored as potential energy in the configuration of the system. <<POINT:config-2-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> Potential energy is the universe's way of bookkeeping — it keeps track of energy that's been temporarily traded away from motion and stored in the shape of a system, ready to be reclaimed. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_6>>
<<FOCUS:block-start>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_6:round_trip_diagram>> Here's something strange: push a block across a table and back to exactly where it started — same position, same everything. Yet the universe has changed. Energy is gone. Where did it go, and why can't you get it back? <<FOCUS:friction-right-leg>> Watch the outward leg first. The block slides right. Friction? It always opposes motion — so friction points left, doing negative work on the block. <<TRACE:friction-right-leg>> <<FOCUS:friction-left-leg>> Now the block comes back. Motion is now leftward — so friction flips and points right. But it's STILL opposing motion, so it STILL does negative work. <<TRACE:friction-left-leg>> <<FOCUS:total-work-label>> Add it up: negative on the way out, negative on the way back. The total work done by friction over the full round trip is minus two µmgl — never zero. <<PAUSE:short>> Each leg contributes negative µmgl, and since there are two legs, the total work by friction is minus two µmgl — always negative, never zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W_{\text{friction, round trip}} = -\mu mg l + (-\mu mg l) = -2\mu mgl|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:spring-block>> Now here's the key question: what if it were a spring instead of friction doing the work? After a full round trip, would the spring also drain energy? <<PAUSE:long>> Watch this spring-block system. The block passes through point A — the equilibrium — with speed v-zero on its first pass. It bounces, comes back, and passes A again. <<TRACE:point-A>> <<POINT:point-A>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:velocity-arrows>> If there were no friction, the second speed at A would be exactly v-zero again. The spring gave back every joule it borrowed. Zero net work over the round trip. <<PAUSE:short>> That's the definition — a conservative force is one that does zero net work over any closed round trip. The spring is conservative. It stores energy and gives it all back. <<POINT:velocity-arrows>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:total-work-label>> Friction is nonconservative. No matter which way the block moves, friction always opposes it — so every single leg of the journey bleeds energy, and the round-trip total is always negative. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> The lost energy doesn't vanish — it becomes heat. But you cannot coax it back into the block's motion. That's why machines with friction grind to a halt, while a frictionless spring can bounce forever. So the dividing line is simple: does the force rob energy on every leg, or does it return what it took? Conservative forces return it all. Nonconservative forces never do. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_7>>
<<FOCUS:ball-top>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_7:ramp_energy_diagram>> A ball sits at the top of a ramp — completely still, doing nothing. Yet somehow it has energy. How can something motionless have energy? The answer is: it has stored energy — energy locked in its position, in how it's arranged relative to the Earth. We call this potential energy. <<POINT:ball-top>> <<FOCUS:gravity-arrow>> Now here's the key question: how much potential energy does it have? To answer that, we ask — what would gravity DO if we let the ball go? <<TRACE:gravity-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ramp-slope>> Gravity would do positive work pulling it down the ramp. And here's the definition: the potential energy DECREASES by exactly that amount of work. In other words, ΔU equals negative W. <<TRACE:ramp-slope>> <<PAUSE:short>> The change in potential energy is exactly the negative of the work done by the conservative force — whatever work gravity does on the ball, the PE drops by that same amount. <<WRITE_EQUATION:U_f - U_i = -W = -\int_i^f \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}|id=eq-1|boxed>> So when the conservative force does positive work — PE goes down. When it does negative work — PE goes up. The negative sign in the definition captures this perfectly. <<POINT:gravity-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:pe-bar-top>> Now watch what happens to the energy bars as the ball rolls down. At the top: lots of PE, zero KE. <<TRACE:pe-bar-top>> <<FOCUS:ke-bar-bottom>> Halfway down, gravity has done some work — PE has dropped, and that exact amount has appeared as KE. The bars trade height, but notice something. <<TRACE:ke-bar-bottom>> <<FOCUS:total-energy-line>> At the bottom: PE is zero, KE is maximum. And the total — that dashed line — never moved. The sum K plus U is identical at every single point. <<POINT:total-energy-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because PE drops by exactly what KE gains, their sum never changes — the total mechanical energy is conserved. <<WRITE_EQUATION:K_f + U_f = K_i + U_i|id=eq-2|boxed>> This is conservation of mechanical energy: as long as only conservative forces act, kinetic and potential energy swap back and forth freely, but their sum is rock-solid constant. <<POINT:total-energy-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> But what if there's friction? Friction is non-conservative — it doesn't store energy, it bleeds it away as heat. The total K plus U shrinks. Conservation of mechanical energy breaks down. <<FOCUS:total-energy-line>> So the rule has one clean condition: conservative forces only. Meet that condition, and you get the most powerful shortcut in mechanics — you never have to track force and acceleration step by step. Just check the total energy at start and finish. <<POINT:total-energy-line>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_8>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> When you pick up a wooden block and slide it across a table, does the energy stored inside the block — between its atoms — change at all? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_8:rigid_body_two_particles>> Let's find out. Meet a rigid body — any solid object where every pair of atoms inside stays the exact same distance apart, no matter how the object moves. <<TRACE:rigid-body-outline>> <<FOCUS:separation-label>> Pick any two particles inside — call them A and B. The one thing a rigid body guarantees is that this separation between them never changes. <<POINT:separation-label>> Now, A and B push and pull on each other — those are internal forces. By Newton's third law, the force A exerts on B is exactly equal and opposite to the force B exerts on A. <<TRACE:force-AB>> <<TRACE:force-AB>> Here's the beautiful part — because the body is rigid, when the block moves, A and B move by the exact same displacement. Both shift by the same amount, in the same direction. <<TRACE:displacement-A>> <<TRACE:displacement-A>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-BA>> <<FOCUS:force-BA>> So the work done by F_AB adds up with the work done by F_BA. Since the forces are equal and opposite but the displacements are identical, they cancel perfectly — the total work by internal forces is zero. <<PAUSE:short>> Since the two forces are equal and opposite and both particles move by the same displacement, the two work contributions cancel — let's write that out precisely. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W = \int (\vec{F}_{AB} \cdot d\vec{r}_A + \vec{F}_{BA} \cdot d\vec{r}_B) = \int (\vec{F}_{AB} + \vec{F}_{BA}) \cdot d\vec{r}_A = 0|id=eq-1|boxed>> And remember — potential energy only changes when work is done against an internal force. No internal work means no change in internal potential energy. <<POINT:separation-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So here's the answer to our opening question: slide the block, spin it, toss it — the energy stored between its atoms stays exactly the same. The internal potential energy of a rigid body is frozen. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> This means whenever we calculate how potential energy changes in a problem, we only need to watch the separations between objects — like a ball and the Earth — not what's happening inside the objects themselves.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_9>>
<<FOCUS:block-low>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_9:lift_diagram>> If you lift a book above your head and hold it perfectly still — you're not moving, the book isn't moving — is there any energy in this system at all? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes — and here's the key insight: you did work getting it up there, and that work didn't vanish. It got stored, like a battery charging up, waiting to be released the moment you let go. <<TRACE:height-arrow>> <<FOCUS:block-high>> Watch what happens as we lift the block. There's the block at the ground — and now we raise it through a height h. <<TRACE:block-high>> While lifting, we push up with force F, and gravity pulls down with force mg. These two are equal and opposite — so the block moves up steadily. <<POINT:lift-force-arrow>> <<POINT:lift-force-arrow>> <<FOCUS:pe-label>> The work we did against gravity — force times distance — is exactly mgh. And that's precisely the gravitational potential energy now stored in the Earth-plus-block system. <<PAUSE:short>> The work done lifting a mass m through height h is force times distance — that's mg times h. That exact amount is the gravitational potential energy now stored in the system. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Delta PE = mgh|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:ground-level>> Now here's a question that trips people up: where exactly is the zero? Where does the potential energy equal nothing? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Wherever you decide! The ground, the floor, the bottom of a cliff — you pick the reference level, and we call PE zero there. Only changes in PE ever matter physically. <<POINT:ground-level>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:height-arrow>> So if you set the ground as your zero, a block of mass m at height h has gravitational PE equal to mgh above it. Raise it higher — store more energy. Drop it back — that energy is released. <<TRACE:height-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Technically, this energy lives in the whole Earth-block system — the Earth's gravity is the thing creating it. But since the Earth barely moves, we just say the block has the potential energy. That's a convenient shorthand, not a sloppy one. <<POINT:gravity-force-arrow>> One last thing to lock in: PE = mgh only works when h is small compared to Earth's radius — close to the surface, where g is essentially constant. That's the world most problems live in. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_10>>
<<FOCUS:spring-coil>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_10:spring_diagram>> If you squash a spring and let go, it launches things — but while it's squashed, nothing is moving. So where is the energy hiding? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's our setup: a spring fixed to a wall on the left, with a block attached to its free end on the right. <<TRACE:spring-coil>> <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> We slowly pull the block to the right, stretching the spring by a distance x from its natural length. <<TRACE:displacement-arrow>> As we pull, we're doing work on the spring — we're forcing energy INTO it. But the spring has no mass, so it can't have kinetic energy. <<POINT:spring-coil>> <<PAUSE:short>> That energy has nowhere else to go — it gets locked up inside the spring itself, in the tiny internal forces between its coils. This stored energy is called elastic potential energy. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-arrow-block>> Now here's the key question: how much energy gets stored? It depends on two things — how stiff the spring is, and how far you've stretched it. <<POINT:force-arrow-block>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> The spring pulls back with a force kx — k is the spring constant, a measure of stiffness, and x is the stretch. A stiffer spring or a bigger stretch means more stored energy. <<POINT:displacement-arrow>> To find the total work done in stretching from zero to x, we add up all those tiny force contributions — and the result is half of k times x squared. <<TRACE:displacement-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> The energy stored is half of the spring constant multiplied by the square of the stretch distance. <<WRITE_EQUATION:U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:spring-coil>> So the elastic potential energy stored equals ½kx². Notice that x is squared — stretch it twice as far and you store FOUR times the energy, not twice. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> And the same formula works whether the spring is stretched OR compressed — the energy stored is always ½kx², always positive, always waiting to be released. <<POINT:spring-coil>> <<FOCUS:spring-coil>> So the answer to our opening question: the energy hides inside the spring as elastic potential energy — invisible, motionless, but absolutely real — equal to ½kx².

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:work_and_energy:8_11>>
<<FOCUS:thermal-energy-node>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:8_11:energy_forms_map>> A hot cup of tea sitting perfectly still on a table — it's not moving, nothing's falling. So where is its energy hiding? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Inside that tea, billions of water molecules are vibrating and bouncing around at high speed, and they're pushing and pulling on each other — that microscopic chaos IS energy, called thermal or internal energy. <<TRACE:thermal-energy-node>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mechanical-energy-node>> You already know two forms: kinetic energy — energy of motion — and potential energy — energy stored by position. Together they make mechanical energy. So energy comes in very different flavours — thermal, mechanical — and that list keeps growing. <<POINT:mechanical-energy-node>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:chemical-energy-node>> When wood burns, a chemical reaction releases energy as heat and light — that's chemical energy converting into other forms. <<FOCUS:light-sound-node>> A guitar string vibrating sends sound energy through the air; the Sun blasts light energy across space — both are real, measurable forms of energy. <<FOCUS:mass-energy-node>> Now here's the wildest one: Einstein discovered that mass itself is a form of energy. A particle sitting completely still, doing nothing, still holds enormous energy locked inside its mass. How enormous? Destroying a single electron — a speck far too small to see — releases about 8 × 10⁻¹⁴ joules. That sounds tiny, but scale it up and you get nuclear reactions powering stars. So energy exists in many forms: kinetic, potential, thermal, chemical, light, sound, and mass itself — each completely real and measurable. <<TRACE:connecting-arrows>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mass-energy-node>> Einstein showed that mass itself is a form of energy — a tiny amount of mass is equivalent to an enormous amount of energy, because it gets multiplied by the speed of light squared. Einstein showed that mass itself is a form of energy — a tiny amount of mass is equivalent to an enormous amount of energy, because it gets multiplied by the speed of light squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = mc^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:conservation-centre>> Now, here's the big question: energy keeps changing form — mechanical to thermal, chemical to light — so does the total amount of energy in the universe ever change? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Never. Not once, not ever. Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transformed from one form into another. The total always stays the same. <<TRACE:conservation-centre>> <<PAUSE:short>> This is the generalised law of conservation of energy — it works because ALL forms of energy are counted, not just mechanical ones. <<POINT:conservation-centre>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<FOCUS:suspension-point-O>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:work_and_energy:4_9 m:pendulum_slack_diagram>> A pendulum swings up, its string goes completely limp mid-air — and somehow the ball curves back and passes through the exact point it was hanging from. How on earth does that happen? <<FOCUS:circular-arc>> Here's the setup. A heavy particle hangs from a string of length l. We give it a sharp horizontal push — speed v₀ — and it swings upward along a circular arc. <<TRACE:circular-arc>> <<FOCUS:point-P>> At some point P along the arc, the string goes slack. That means the tension has dropped to zero — the string can't push, only pull, so once tension hits zero it's gone. <<FOCUS:weight-vector-P>> Right at that slack moment, the only force left is gravity. Its component pointing toward O — the radial direction — must be exactly what's needed to keep the particle on a circular path, even though the string is limp. <<POINT:weight-vector-P>> <<PAUSE:short>> At the slack point, gravity's component along the string is the only centripetal force — so that component mg cosθ equals mv²/l, giving v² = gl cosθ. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v^2 = gl\cos\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:string-OP>> So here's the key equation at point P: gravity's radial part equals mv²/l. That gives us v² = gl cosθ. The string is slack, and centripetal force is now entirely from gravity. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:circular-arc>> Now, how fast is the particle moving when it reaches P? We use conservation of energy — the kinetic energy it started with minus the gravitational potential energy it gained getting up to P. <<TRACE:circular-arc>> Energy conservation from the bottom to point P gives a second expression for v², and combining it with the slack condition eliminates v, leaving v₀ in terms of θ only. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_0^2 = gl(2 + 3\cos\theta)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Combining energy conservation with our slack condition, we get v₀² in terms of θ: v₀² = gl(2 + 3cosθ). But we still don't know θ — that's where the parabola comes in. <<POINT:angle-theta>> <<FOCUS:parabolic-path>> Once the string goes slack at P, the particle becomes a free projectile — gravity only, no string. It follows a perfect parabola from P back up to O. <<TRACE:parabolic-path>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:suspension-point-O>> Here's the clever bit — what angle θ makes the parabola land precisely back at O? Think about it: the horizontal displacement from P to O is l sinθ, and the vertical displacement is −l cosθ. <<POINT:suspension-point-O>> <<PAUSE:long>> Matching the parabola's landing point exactly to O — using both horizontal and vertical projectile equations — forces this unique value of θ. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos\theta = \frac{1}{3}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:point-P>> Setting up the projectile equations for horizontal and vertical motion — with the velocity at P pointing tangentially — and solving, we find that cosθ = 1/3. That's the only angle that threads the ball back through O. Substituting cosθ = 1/3 into v₀² = gl(2 + 3cosθ) gives v₀² = 3gl, so the required initial speed is the square root of 3gl. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_0 = \sqrt{3gl}|id=eq-4|boxed>> Now plug cosθ = 1/3 back into v₀² = gl(2 + 3cosθ), and you get v₀² = gl(2 + 1) = 3gl. So the required launch speed is v₀ = √(3gl). <<POINT:initial-velocity-v0>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Let's zoom out and feel the beauty: one condition locked down θ, a completely different condition locked down v₀ — and they connected through the single moment the string went limp. That's physics telling a precise story. <<TRACE:parabolic-path>> <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding: Sometimes in physics problems, we encounter a situation where an object moves through a specific distance, and that distance becomes the key piece of information we need to calculate work or energy. Imagine you have a block sitting on a surface, and someone pushes it or a spring launches it across a short gap. The distance of half a meter, which is fifty centimeters, might seem small, but it can represent a very meaningful displacement in a problem about work and energy. Remember, work is calculated by multiplying the force applied on an object by the distance through which that force acts, in the direction of the force. So even a modest distance like half a meter, when combined with a force, tells us exactly how much energy has been transferred. Think about pushing a heavy book across a table for just half a meter. You are doing work on that book, and the amount of work depends on how hard you push and how far it travels. In energy problems, this kind of distance measurement often appears as the displacement of an object under the influence of gravity, a spring, friction, or an applied force. The half meter distance is not just a number sitting there, it is the bridge between force and energy. It tells us over what span the force was active. Whether we are talking about a ball rolling down a ramp, a weight being lifted, or a compressed spring releasing its stored energy, the distance traveled is always central to the story. Keep this in mind as you work through problems: always identify the displacement clearly, make sure it lines up with the direction of the force, and then you have everything you need to find the work done.
examples: Imagine you are lifting a small bag of apples straight up by half a meter, which is about the height from your waist to your shoulder. The force you apply is equal to the weight of the bag, and the distance is half a meter. Multiply those two together and you get the work you did on the bag. That work is exactly equal to the gravitational potential energy the bag gained by being raised higher. A short distance, but real energy was transferred.

Think about a toy car being pushed by a compressed spring. The spring pushes the car over a distance of half a meter before losing contact. All the energy stored in the spring gets converted into the kinetic energy of the moving car over that half meter stretch. The distance here is the length over which the spring force acts, and it is crucial for calculating how much energy the car receives.

Picture a hockey puck sliding along an ice surface. If friction acts on it over a distance of half a meter, that friction force does negative work on the puck, slowing it down. The energy lost by the puck equals the friction force multiplied by the half meter distance. Even though the puck only travels a short way, energy is definitely being removed from it and converted into heat.

Consider a construction worker lowering a brick straight down by half a meter using a rope. Gravity pulls the brick downward and the brick moves downward, so gravity does positive work on the brick over that half meter. Meanwhile the rope tension does negative work. The net work done on the brick equals the change in its kinetic energy. Half a meter is enough distance to make a meaningful difference in how fast the brick is moving by the time it reaches the lower position.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, let's dig into one of the most beautiful and tricky problems in circular motion and energy — a pendulum where the string goes slack mid-swing, and the particle then flies through the air like a projectile. This is a wonderful example of how conservation of energy and Newton's laws work together to solve something that looks impossibly complicated at first glance. Here is the setup: a heavy particle hangs from a string of length l. We give it a horizontal push with some initial speed, which we want to find. The particle swings upward, and at some point the string goes slack — meaning the string can no longer pull, so the tension drops to zero. From that moment on, the only force acting is gravity, and the particle follows a curved parabolic path through the air. The remarkable condition we are given is that this parabolic path must carry the particle exactly back through the point where it started — the point of suspension at the top of the string. So we have two big tools to use. First, at the exact moment the string goes slack, the centripetal force needed to keep the particle moving in a circle must equal the component of gravity pulling inward along the string. This gives us a relationship between the speed at that point and the angle the string makes with the upward vertical. Second, conservation of energy connects the initial speed at the bottom to the speed at the point where the string goes slack. Once we combine these two equations, we get the speed and angle at the moment of release into the parabola. Then we treat the rest of the journey as projectile motion — horizontal and vertical equations of motion — and apply the condition that the particle passes through the suspension point. Working through all of this carefully, we find that the tangent of the angle must equal the square root of two, and the required initial speed turns out to be the square root of the quantity g times l times the sum of two and the square root of three. What makes this problem so satisfying is that it chains together circular motion, energy conservation, and projectile motion all in one elegant solution. Each piece of physics hands off to the next, like a relay race.
examples: Think about a ball on a string that you swing in a vertical circle. As long as the string is taut, the string pulls the ball inward toward your hand. But if the ball slows down too much near the top, the string goes limp — it can only pull, not push. At that instant, the ball is released into free flight under gravity alone, just like a ball thrown into the air. In our problem, this slack point happens somewhere on the way up, not necessarily at the top, and we have to figure out exactly where.

Here is a helpful everyday picture. Imagine you are on a swing at a playground. If someone pushes you just hard enough, you might swing up to a point where the chains go loose and you briefly become airborne before falling back down. If the push were perfectly calculated, you could theoretically arc through the air and land right back on the seat where you started. That is essentially what this problem is asking — what is the exact push needed so the particle lands precisely back at the pivot point after the string goes slack?

The two-step energy argument is worth pausing on. At the bottom, the particle has kinetic energy from its initial speed. As it rises, it trades kinetic energy for gravitational potential energy — it slows down as it goes higher. We measure the height gained from the bottom, which is the length of the string plus the vertical distance from the center to the slack point. Conservation of energy says the total of kinetic and potential energy stays the same throughout, so we can write the speed at any height in terms of the initial speed. This is the key bridge between the starting conditions and the slack point.

Once the string goes slack, the particle is essentially a ball thrown at an angle from a certain height — a classic projectile. We know its position and velocity at the moment of release, and we need it to pass through a specific target point, which is the suspension point directly above where it started. We write out the horizontal distance traveled and the vertical distance traveled in terms of time, set them equal to the coordinates of the suspension point, and solve. The condition that both equations are satisfied simultaneously is what pins down the angle and, working backward, the initial speed.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about kinetic energy — the energy something has simply because it is moving. Think about a sleeping person versus someone running around on a dance floor. The runner has something extra going on, and in physics we give that 'something extra' a name: kinetic energy. We define it as one half times the mass of the object times its speed squared. So the faster something moves, or the heavier it is, the more kinetic energy it carries. Both mass and speed matter, but speed matters even more because it gets squared — double the speed and you get four times the kinetic energy. That's a really important idea to sit with for a moment. For a whole system of objects, like all the molecules in a bouncing ball, we just add up the kinetic energies of every single piece. Now, here's a subtle but beautiful point: kinetic energy only changes when the speed changes. If you push something sideways — meaning the force is perfectly perpendicular to the direction of motion — the object curves but its speed stays the same, so its kinetic energy stays the same. Think of a ball swinging in a circle on a string. The string pulls inward, always at a right angle to the motion, and the ball's speed never changes. Kinetic energy is untouched. For kinetic energy to actually change, the force needs to have a component along the direction of motion — what we call a tangential component. When something falls straight down, gravity pulls it in exactly the direction it's moving, so it speeds up and gains kinetic energy. When you throw something straight up, gravity pulls opposite to the motion, so it slows down and loses kinetic energy. The rate at which kinetic energy changes turns out to equal the force times the velocity times the cosine of the angle between them — which is just the dot product of force and velocity. This leads us beautifully into the concept of work, which we'll explore very soon.
examples: Imagine a cricket ball and a tennis ball both moving at the same speed. The cricket ball is much heavier, so it has much more kinetic energy. That's why getting hit by a cricket ball hurts so much more — there's far more energy packed into that moving object. Now imagine the same cricket ball moving twice as fast. Its kinetic energy doesn't just double — it quadruples, because speed is squared in the formula. This is why car crashes at high speed are so much more dangerous than low-speed bumps.

Think about a satellite orbiting the Earth in a perfect circle. Gravity is always pulling the satellite straight toward the center of the Earth, and the satellite is always moving sideways — so the force and the velocity are always at a right angle to each other. Because of this, the satellite's speed never changes, and its kinetic energy stays perfectly constant the whole time it orbits. No energy is gained, none is lost. The force is real, but it does nothing to the kinetic energy.

Picture a skateboarder rolling down a ramp. As they go down, gravity has a component pushing them forward along the slope — in the same direction they're moving. So they speed up, and their kinetic energy grows. Now they hit a flat section and start going up the other side of the ramp. Now gravity is pulling them back while they're still moving forward — opposite directions — so they slow down and their kinetic energy decreases. At the very top of the other side, if they make it, they've converted most of that kinetic energy into something else entirely.

Consider two identical toy cars. One is sitting still on a table, and one is rolling across it at a steady speed. The rolling car has kinetic energy — one half times its mass times its speed squared. If no force acts on it, that kinetic energy stays exactly the same forever. It won't speed up or slow down on its own. Only a force — like friction from the table, or a push from your hand — can change how much kinetic energy it has. This is a direct consequence of Newton's first law working hand in hand with our definition of kinetic energy.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most powerful ideas in all of physics — the work-energy theorem. First, what is work? In everyday life, we use the word 'work' loosely, but in physics it has a very precise meaning. When a force acts on an object and that object moves, the work done by that force is the force multiplied by the distance moved, but only counting the part of the force that actually points in the direction of motion. So if you push something at an angle, only the component of your push that lines up with the movement counts. That's where the cosine comes in when we describe it in words — work equals force times distance times the cosine of the angle between them.

Now here's the beautiful part — the work-energy theorem. If you add up all the work done on a particle by every single force acting on it, that total equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. In other words, work done equals final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy. Think about that for a moment. Every time something speeds up or slows down, it's because forces have done work on it. This gives us a direct bridge between forces and motion — not through acceleration, but through energy.

An important subtlety: the work done by just one individual force, say friction alone or gravity alone, does not equal the change in kinetic energy. It's only when you add up the work from all the forces together — the net work — that you get the change in kinetic energy. Each force contributes its own share of work, and those shares add up.

Finally, let's talk about power. Power is simply how fast work is being done. If you do a lot of work very quickly, you're delivering a lot of power. Mathematically, power equals force dotted with velocity — meaning force times speed, again only counting the component in the direction of motion. The unit of power is the watt, which is one joule of work per second. You've probably seen watts on light bulbs. Another unit you might hear is horsepower, which equals 746 watts — that's used a lot when talking about car engines.
examples: Imagine you're pushing a heavy box across the floor. Two forces are acting on it horizontally — your push forward and friction pushing backward. Your push does positive work because it acts in the direction of motion. Friction does negative work because it acts opposite to the motion. The change in the box's kinetic energy equals the sum of both — your work plus friction's work. If friction's work exactly cancels yours, the box moves at constant speed and the net change in kinetic energy is zero. That's the work-energy theorem in action.

Think about a ball being thrown straight up into the air. As it rises, gravity pulls it downward while it moves upward, so gravity does negative work on it — it's slowing the ball down. The ball's kinetic energy decreases. When the ball falls back down, gravity now acts in the same direction as motion, doing positive work, and the ball speeds up again. The work done by gravity directly tells you how much kinetic energy the ball gains or loses. No need to track acceleration at every instant — just track the work.

Here's a great everyday example of power. Two students carry identical backpacks up the same flight of stairs. They do the same amount of work — same force, same distance. But one student runs up in 5 seconds and the other walks up in 20 seconds. The runner delivers four times more power, even though the total work is identical. This is exactly what power measures — not how much work, but how quickly that work gets done. A car engine with more horsepower doesn't necessarily do more total work, it just does it faster.

Consider a car braking to a stop. The brakes apply a friction force opposite to the direction of motion. This force does negative work on the car. According to the work-energy theorem, the car's kinetic energy must decrease by exactly the amount of work done by that braking force. This is why heavier cars or faster cars are harder to stop — they have more kinetic energy, so the brakes need to do more work to bring that kinetic energy down to zero.

Let's talk about how we actually calculate the work done by a force, because the formula changes depending on what kind of force we're dealing with. The big idea is this: work equals force times displacement times the cosine of the angle between them. That cosine part is crucial — it tells us how much of the force is actually acting in the direction of motion. If the force and displacement point in exactly the same direction, cosine of zero degrees is one, so you get the full product. If they're perpendicular, cosine of ninety degrees is zero, meaning no work is done at all. Think about that — a force can be pushing on something and still do zero work if it's pushing sideways to the motion.

Now, this simple formula works beautifully when the force is constant — same size, same direction throughout the whole journey. Gravity near Earth's surface is a perfect example. When something falls a height h, gravity does work equal to mass times g times h. Here's something elegant: it doesn't matter what path the object takes to get from point A to point B. Whether it falls straight down or slides down a winding ramp, gravity does the same amount of work — it only cares about the vertical height descended. And if the object goes up and comes back down to the same spot, gravity does zero net work over that round trip.

But what about a spring? A spring force is trickier because it changes as the spring stretches or compresses — the more you stretch it, the harder it pulls back. So we can't just multiply force by displacement directly. Instead, we add up tiny little bits of work over tiny displacements, which is what integration does for us. The result is that the work done by a spring force equals one half times the spring constant times the displacement squared. Notice the sign matters here: when you stretch or compress a spring away from its natural length, the spring force opposes your motion, so the work done by the spring on you is negative. When the spring returns to its natural length, it does positive work. And just like gravity, a spring does zero net work over a complete round trip — stretch it and bring it back, and the work cancels out perfectly. These two forces — gravity and spring force — share this beautiful property, and we'll see later that it connects deeply to the idea of stored energy.
examples: Imagine you're pushing a heavy box across the floor, and you push at an angle — say you're leaning into it with your arms pointing downward at thirty degrees below horizontal. The floor is horizontal, so only the horizontal part of your push actually moves the box forward. The vertical part of your push just presses the box into the floor and does no useful work. This is exactly what the cosine of the angle accounts for. If you pushed perfectly horizontally, all your effort would go into moving the box. The more you angle downward, the less efficient your push becomes.

Think about a ball thrown straight up into the air. As it rises, gravity pulls it downward but the ball moves upward — they're in opposite directions, so the angle between force and displacement is one hundred eighty degrees, and cosine of one hundred eighty is negative one. Gravity does negative work on the way up, slowing the ball down. On the way back down, gravity and motion are in the same direction, so it does positive work, speeding the ball up. By the time the ball returns to your hand at the same height, the total work done by gravity is exactly zero — the negative and positive parts cancel perfectly.

Now picture a spring attached to a wall with a block sitting against its free end on a smooth table. When the spring is at its natural length, it exerts no force. But as you push the block and compress the spring by two centimetres, the spring pushes back harder and harder the more you compress it. Because the spring force and the block's displacement are in opposite directions the whole time, the spring does negative work on the block as you compress it. The work done equals one half times the spring constant times the compression squared. For a spring constant of fifty newtons per metre compressed by one centimetre, that works out to two and a half thousandths of a joule — small but real.

Here's a lovely case where a force does zero work: a ball on a string swinging in a horizontal circle. The string always pulls the ball toward the centre of the circle, but the ball always moves along the circle — sideways, never toward or away from the centre. The tension in the string and the velocity of the ball are always perpendicular to each other. Cosine of ninety degrees is zero, so the string tension does absolutely no work on the ball, even though it's clearly exerting a force. This is why the ball's speed stays constant in circular motion — no work means no change in energy.

topics.our_understanding: So far we have been thinking about a single particle — one object, one force, one change in kinetic energy. The work-energy theorem tells us that the total work done on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy. Simple enough. But now let's ask a bigger question: what happens when we have a whole system of particles that are pushing or pulling on each other? This is where things get really interesting. Imagine two charged particles — one positive and one negative — sitting in space near each other. They attract each other. Nobody from the outside is pushing them. Yet they start moving toward each other, speeding up, gaining kinetic energy. How? Where did that energy come from? Here is the key insight. Even though there is no external force, the particles are exerting forces on each other — these are called internal forces. Particle B pulls on particle A, and as A moves toward B, that pull does work on A, increasing A's kinetic energy. At the same time, particle A pulls on particle B, and as B moves toward A, that pull does work on B too. Now here is something subtle that trips a lot of people up. The two forces are equal in size but opposite in direction — that is Newton's third law. You might think the work they do would cancel out to zero. But think carefully about the displacements. Both particles are moving toward each other, so both displacements are also in opposite directions. A force and a displacement that are both reversed still give you a positive result for work. So both forces do positive work, and the total kinetic energy of the system goes up. The big takeaway is this: for a system of particles, the change in total kinetic energy equals the work done by all forces — both the external forces coming from outside the system and the internal forces the particles exert on each other. Internal forces absolutely matter when we are tracking energy in a system.
examples: Think about two magnets placed close together with opposite poles facing each other. They attract. If you let them go, they fly toward each other and speed up. No one is pushing them from outside. The force that magnet A exerts on magnet B does positive work on B, and the force that magnet B exerts on magnet A does positive work on A. Both internal forces contribute, and the total kinetic energy of the two-magnet system increases. This is exactly the idea — internal forces can change the kinetic energy of a system.

Now imagine two ice skaters standing still on a frictionless rink, facing each other. One skater pushes the other. They both glide away in opposite directions, both gaining kinetic energy. The push between them is an internal force within the two-skater system. Even though the forces on each skater are equal and opposite, both skaters move in directions that match their own force, so both forces do positive work. The total kinetic energy of the system goes from zero to something positive — all because of an internal force.

Here is why the cancellation argument fails. Suppose force on A points to the right, and force on B points to the left — equal and opposite, so they add to zero as vectors. But A moves to the left toward B, and B moves to the right toward A. Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force. For A, the force and displacement are both leftward — positive work. For B, the force and displacement are both rightward — positive work again. The vector forces cancel, but the scalar works add up. That distinction between vectors and scalars is crucial here.

Consider a firecracker sitting still. Its total momentum is zero and its kinetic energy is zero. When it explodes, the pieces fly outward in all directions. The explosion forces are all internal to the firecracker system. Yet the total kinetic energy of all the pieces is now large and positive. The internal forces of the explosion did work on all the pieces, increasing the system's kinetic energy dramatically. This shows that internal forces can be enormously important in changing how much kinetic energy a system has.

topics.our_understanding: Let me paint a picture for you. Imagine two electrically charged particles floating in space, and they attract each other — kind of like two magnets pulling toward one another. Now suppose at some moment, both particles are moving away from each other. What happens? The attraction between them acts like a gentle brake, slowing them both down. As they slow down, their kinetic energy — the energy of motion — is decreasing. So where is that energy going? Is it just disappearing? That would be very strange, and in fact, it does not disappear at all. Here is the beautiful part: if you simply wait, the particles slow to a stop, then get pulled back toward each other, speed up again, and eventually return to exactly where they started — moving at exactly the same speeds as before. The kinetic energy is fully restored. So the energy was not lost. It was stored somewhere, waiting to come back. That stored energy is what we call potential energy. Think of potential energy as energy that depends on the arrangement, or configuration, of the objects in a system — how far apart they are, how they are positioned relative to each other. When the particles moved apart and slowed down, kinetic energy was converted into potential energy. When they came back together and sped up, that potential energy converted right back into kinetic energy. The total — kinetic plus potential — stayed the same throughout. This is a profound idea. Energy can change its form, shifting back and forth between motion and stored configuration, but the total amount is conserved. This concept of potential energy is going to be one of the most powerful tools you will use in physics, and it all starts with this simple observation: sometimes energy seems to hide, but it always comes back.
examples: Think about stretching a rubber band. As you pull the two ends apart, your hands slow down and stop — you have done work against the elastic force. The kinetic energy of your hands goes to zero, but the energy is not gone. It is stored as potential energy in the stretched rubber band. The moment you let go, that stored energy converts back into kinetic energy as the rubber band snaps back. The configuration — how stretched the band is — determines how much potential energy is stored.

Imagine rolling a ball up a hill. As it climbs, it slows down — kinetic energy is decreasing. But when it rolls back down, it speeds up again and returns to its original speed at the bottom. The energy was not lost while the ball was high up on the hill. It was stored as gravitational potential energy, which depends on the ball's height — its configuration relative to the ground. Height up, potential energy up. Height down, kinetic energy back.

Going back to the two charged particles from the section: at the starting moment, both particles are moving apart with certain speeds, giving the system a kinetic energy we can call K-one. As they drift apart against their mutual attraction, they slow down and the kinetic energy drops to a lower value K-two. But the system has not lost energy — it has stored the difference between K-one and K-two as potential energy. When the particles eventually return to their original positions, that potential energy converts back, and the kinetic energy is once again K-one. The sum of kinetic and potential energy never changed throughout the whole journey.

Think of a swing at a playground. At the very top of its arc, the swing moves slowly — almost no kinetic energy. But it has a lot of potential energy because of its height. At the very bottom of the arc, it moves fastest — maximum kinetic energy — and its height is lowest, so potential energy is at its minimum. Energy is constantly trading between these two forms as the swing goes back and forth, but the total stays the same. That trade-off between kinetic and potential energy is exactly the idea introduced here.

topics.our_understanding:
Today we're going to talk about one of the most important distinctions in all of physics — the difference between conservative and nonconservative forces. This idea helps us understand why some machines can keep running smoothly while others grind to a halt.

Imagine you push a block across a rough table to the right, and then push it back to where it started. You've made a round trip — the block is exactly where it began. Now ask yourself: what did friction do during that journey? When the block moved right, friction pulled it left, doing negative work. When the block moved back left, friction pulled it right — still doing negative work. So after the full round trip, friction has done a total negative amount of work. Energy has been lost, and it's gone as heat. You can never get it back just by returning to the starting point.

Now think about a spring. If you stretch a spring and let it pull a block back to where it started, the spring does positive work on the way back that exactly cancels the negative work it did on the way out. The total work done by the spring in a round trip is zero. That's the key idea.

A force is called conservative if the total work it does in any round trip is always zero. Another way to say the same thing is this: a conservative force only cares about where you start and where you end — it doesn't matter which path you took to get there. Gravity works this way. The spring force works this way. Coulomb's electric force works this way.

Friction is the classic example of a nonconservative force. It always opposes motion, so no matter which direction you travel, friction is always stealing energy. The longer the path, the more energy is lost. So the work done by friction absolutely depends on the path you take, not just your start and end points.

This distinction matters enormously. In systems with only conservative forces, energy can be stored and fully recovered. In systems with nonconservative forces like friction, energy leaks away permanently as heat, and eventually motion stops. Think about the spring-and-block example — every time the block passes through the middle, it's moving a little slower, because friction has been quietly draining energy the whole time.
examples: Think about lifting a book from the floor to a shelf. Gravity does negative work as you lift it. Now drop the book — gravity does positive work as it falls back down. The total work done by gravity for that round trip, up and then back down to the same height, is exactly zero. It doesn't matter if you carried the book in a straight line or walked around the room first. Gravity only cares about the height difference between start and finish. That's what makes gravity a conservative force.

Now imagine sliding a heavy box across a carpet from one side of the room to the other, and then sliding it back. Friction acts against you both ways. On the way there, friction does negative work. On the way back, friction does negative work again. The total work done by friction is negative — not zero. And if you took a longer, winding path instead of a straight line, friction would steal even more energy. The work depends on the path length, which is the hallmark of a nonconservative force.

Picture a block attached to a spring on a rough table. You pull the block to one side and release it. It swings through the middle position with a certain speed, goes to the other side, and comes back. When it passes through the middle again, it's moving slower than before. The spring is conservative — it gives back all the energy it stored. But friction is nonconservative — it has been quietly taking energy away on every part of the journey and converting it to heat. Given enough time, the block stops completely. If there were no friction at all, the block would keep swinging back and forth forever at the same speed.

Think about a roller coaster with perfectly smooth, frictionless tracks. A car that starts at the top of a hill will always return to exactly that same height on the other side, because gravity is conservative and no energy is lost. But real roller coasters have friction. Every loop and curve bleeds a little energy away as heat. That's why real roller coasters always end lower than they start — the nonconservative force of friction has permanently taken some energy out of the system.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, let's talk about one of the most powerful ideas in all of physics — the conservation of mechanical energy. We've already met kinetic energy, which is the energy of motion. Now we're bringing in potential energy, which you can think of as stored energy — energy that a system has because of its configuration, or the way its parts are arranged relative to each other. Here's the key definition: the change in potential energy as a system moves from one arrangement to another is equal to the negative of the work done by the conservative internal forces during that change. The negative sign is crucial — when a conservative force does positive work on a system, the potential energy decreases, and vice versa. Think of a ball falling — gravity does positive work, and the gravitational potential energy goes down while kinetic energy goes up. Now, when you add kinetic energy and potential energy together, you get what we call the total mechanical energy. The beautiful result is this: if all the internal forces in a system are conservative — like gravity or spring forces — and no external forces are doing work, then the total mechanical energy stays the same throughout the motion. It doesn't matter what happens in between. This is the principle of conservation of mechanical energy. However, if nonconservative forces like friction are involved, mechanical energy is not conserved — some of it gets converted to heat or sound. In that case, we can still use the work-energy theorem, which always holds. We write that the work done by nonconservative forces plus the work done by external forces equals the change in total mechanical energy. One more thing worth noting: we only ever define a change in potential energy, not an absolute value. Just like you can choose any point as your zero on a number line, you can choose any configuration as your zero potential energy. That freedom is actually very useful.
examples: Imagine you hold a ball at a height above the ground and let it go. As it falls, gravity — a conservative force — does work on it. The ball speeds up, so kinetic energy increases. At the same time, gravitational potential energy decreases by exactly the same amount. If you add them together at any point during the fall, you always get the same total. That's conservation of mechanical energy in action. The moment the ball hits the ground and bounces with less height each time, friction and air resistance — nonconservative forces — are stealing away some mechanical energy, which is why the total no longer stays constant.

Think about a compressed spring launching a toy car on a frictionless track. Before release, the car is still — all the energy is stored as elastic potential energy in the spring. The moment you let go, the spring does work on the car, converting that potential energy into kinetic energy. If the track is truly frictionless, the total mechanical energy — kinetic plus potential — stays exactly the same throughout. This is a perfect example of conservative internal forces at work, with no external forces doing anything extra.

In the charged particle example we worked through, particle B is repelled by particle A and flies away. The repulsive force between them is conservative, and the force holding A in place does no work because A never moves. So the total mechanical energy of the system is conserved. We calculated the work done by the repulsive force as B moves very far away, found the change in potential energy from that, and then used conservation of energy to find B's final speed. The answer comes out as the square root of two times k divided by m times r-naught. Notice how powerful this method is — we never had to track the complicated motion step by step.

Here's a real-life contrast to make the idea stick. A skateboarder rolling down a smooth, frictionless ramp converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy perfectly — mechanical energy is conserved. But the same skateboarder on a rough concrete ramp slows down more than expected, because friction is a nonconservative force that converts some mechanical energy into heat. You can actually feel the ramp get slightly warm. In the first case, conservation of mechanical energy applies beautifully. In the second, it doesn't — but the work-energy theorem still tells us exactly how much energy was lost to friction.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about something really elegant in physics — what happens to potential energy when a rigid body moves. A rigid body is just an object where all the parts stay the same distance apart from each other, like a solid metal rod or a wooden block. The atoms inside don't get closer or farther from each other as the object moves around. Now, here's the key question: do the internal forces — the forces that the parts of the object exert on each other — do any work as the object moves? The answer is no, and here's the beautiful reason why. Think about two particles inside a rigid body, let's call them A and B. By Newton's third law, the force that A exerts on B is exactly equal and opposite to the force that B exerts on A. Now, because the body is rigid, both particles move by exactly the same amount in the same direction during any tiny moment of time. So when you add up the work done by both forces, the positive work from one force and the negative work from the other cancel out perfectly, giving you zero total work. This is true whether the body is sliding in a straight line or spinning and rotating — the internal forces always cancel out. And here's why this matters so much for potential energy: potential energy only changes when the distances between interacting particles change. If those distances never change — which is exactly what rigid means — then the potential energy stored in those internal forces never changes either. So when we study how a rigid body moves, we can completely ignore the potential energy between its internal parts. We only need to worry about potential energy coming from outside forces, like gravity. This simplifies our calculations enormously and is one of the reasons the rigid body model is so powerful in physics.
examples: Imagine you pick up a solid brick and carry it across the room. Inside that brick, millions of atoms are pulling and pushing on each other. But because the brick is rigid, none of those atoms get any closer or farther apart during the journey. So all those internal forces do zero work, and the internal potential energy of the brick stays exactly the same. The only energy change you need to think about is the gravitational potential energy, which increases because you lifted the brick higher.

Think about a spinning top. As it rotates, every tiny piece of the top is exerting forces on neighboring pieces. But because the top is rigid, the distances between all those pieces stay constant. The internal forces cancel out in pairs — every push has an equal and opposite push — so they do no net work. You only need to track the top's kinetic energy and its gravitational potential energy, not any internal energy.

Consider two magnets glued firmly together into one rigid object. The magnets pull on each other with strong internal forces. But as you slide this combined object across a table, those internal magnetic forces do no work at all, because the magnets never get closer or farther apart. The potential energy stored between them stays constant throughout the motion. This is exactly why we can treat the whole glued pair as a single object without worrying about what's happening inside.

Here is a way to feel the logic directly. Imagine two friends walking side by side, always staying exactly one meter apart — like a rigid pair. If friend A pushes friend B forward, friend B pushes friend A backward with the same force. But since they both move the same distance at every moment, the work done by A on B and the work done by B on A cancel perfectly. No net energy is transferred between them through those internal pushes. The same logic applies to every pair of particles inside any rigid body.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about gravitational potential energy — one of the most useful ideas in all of physics. Imagine you pick up a heavy book and lift it above your head. You did work to get it up there, and now the book has something stored in it — a kind of energy waiting to be released the moment you let go. That stored energy is what we call gravitational potential energy.

Here's the key idea: when you raise an object of mass m through a height h near the surface of the Earth, the gravitational potential energy of the system increases by m times g times h. When the object comes back down by that same height, that energy is released. Simple and powerful.

Now, technically this energy belongs to the whole system — the Earth and the object together. The Earth's gravity is what creates this energy in the first place. But because the Earth is so enormously massive compared to any object we deal with, the Earth barely moves at all. So for convenience, we just say the potential energy belongs to the object. That's a perfectly fine shortcut.

Here's another beautiful thing: you get to choose where the zero level is. You can say the ground floor of a building is your zero, or the tabletop, or even the floor below you. It doesn't matter, because what we actually use in calculations is the change in potential energy, not the absolute value. Pick whatever reference point makes your problem easiest.

Now here's where it gets really useful. If no outside forces are doing work on a system — like when a block slides down a frictionless ramp or a pendulum swings freely — then the total mechanical energy stays constant. That means any decrease in potential energy must show up as an increase in kinetic energy, and vice versa. This conservation of mechanical energy lets us find speeds at different heights without ever worrying about the details of the path taken. The shape of the ramp doesn't matter. Only the height difference does. That's a remarkably powerful result.
examples: Think about a roller coaster car released from the top of a hill. As it rolls down, it loses height, so its gravitational potential energy decreases. That lost potential energy converts into kinetic energy — the car speeds up. Using m times g times h, you can calculate exactly how fast the car is moving at the bottom, as long as friction is small enough to ignore. The twists and turns of the track don't matter at all — only the vertical drop counts.

A block is released from rest at the top of a smooth, frictionless curved ramp and slides down to a lower point. The height difference between the two points is h. Since the surface is frictionless, no energy is lost to heat. The potential energy lost — m times g times h — becomes kinetic energy at the bottom. Setting one-half times m times v squared equal to m times g times h, and cancelling the mass from both sides, gives v equals the square root of two times g times h. Notice the mass cancels — a heavy block and a light block reach the same speed at the bottom.

A pendulum bob swings from its lowest point upward. At the lowest point it moves fastest, and as it rises, it slows down. The height it reaches above the lowest point is found using the length of the string and the angle it makes with the vertical. The increase in height equals the string length times the quantity one minus the cosine of the angle. Using conservation of energy, you can find the speed at any angle just by tracking how much height the bob has gained. The string never does any work because it always pulls sideways, perpendicular to the motion.

Think about dropping your phone from different heights. If you drop it from one metre, it hits the ground with a certain speed. If you drop it from four metres — four times the height — the potential energy is four times greater, so the kinetic energy at the bottom is four times greater too. But kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so the speed only doubles. This is why the damage from dropping something from a greater height grows much faster than you might expect — speed doubles when height quadruples.
